name: Lean bulk
lead: A lean bulk, also called a clean bulk or lean gaining, is a muscle-building phase that combines resistance training with a small calorie surplus, so a person adds muscle while limiting fat gain.[1][2] It is aimed at a fuller, more muscular physique that still looks defined, and in looksmaxxing circles at building shoulders, chest and arms without a soft or bloated face.[4][5]

It takes longer than a large-surplus approach, the so-called dirty bulk, but is described as more precise.[1] A Grokipedia summary gives a surplus of about 250 to 500 kcal per day above maintenance, protein of 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg per day, weekly weight checks to keep gains near 0.25 to 0.5 kg per week, and about 3 to 6 kg of muscle per year for intermediate lifters, while noting that some of its own figures conflict across sections.[2]

Research on the question is limited but growing. A 2023 trial in resistance-trained people found that an 8-week surplus of 15 percent produced more skinfold fat gain than maintenance, with no clear difference in muscle thickness between groups, which is the kind of result lean-bulk advocates cite.[3] A 2019 review in Frontiers in Nutrition asked whether an energy surplus is required to maximise hypertrophy at all, and concluded that the surplus needed is unknown.[8] Looksmax.org posters ask about surplus size, whether a lean bulk will cause bloating or fat gain in the face, and whether to start one straight after a cut.[4][5][9]

angle.text: Lifters eat slightly above maintenance and train progressively, weighing weekly to keep gains slow. The aim is more muscle on the frame, wider shoulders and a fuller physique, with less of the fat that a large surplus adds.

paras: Bulking means eating in a calorie surplus to support muscle growth, and the surplus size influences how much fat accompanies the gain.[1] Wikipedia says most present-day bodybuilding competitors gain muscle in an off-season and then cut fat for about 12 to 14 weeks before a contest.[1] A clean or lean bulk keeps the surplus small and food choices controlled, which is said to take longer but be more precise, and often alternates higher- and lower-calorie days with moderate carbohydrate and protein and low fat.[1]

A dirty bulk uses a large surplus, often from calorie-dense foods and without tracking macronutrients, for faster weight gain; Wikipedia says it can add muscle quickly but also significant fat and usually needs a harsher cut afterwards, and notes that some lifters find it psychologically easier.[1] Grokipedia describes the dirty approach as roughly 500 to 1,000 kcal above maintenance and says it carries more fat gain and a longer cut.[2]

Maintenance calories are commonly estimated with an equation such as Mifflin-St Jeor plus an activity factor.[2] The Mifflin-St Jeor equation was published in 1990 by Mifflin and colleagues, and a review cited by Wikipedia found it about 5 percent more accurate than earlier equations.[11] Web calculators for bulking, cutting and recomposition circulate widely, including a 2026 Show HN project.[2][6]

Wikipedia's muscle hypertrophy article says growth comes mainly from enlargement of existing muscle cells, that a sustained positive energy balance supports anabolism, and that training frequency, intensity and total volume all affect hypertrophy, with progressive overload producing growth.[12] It cites a 2018 review suggesting at least 1.6 g/kg/day of protein for building lean tissue, notes that bodybuilders often recommend more, and cites evidence that intakes above about 1.8 g/kg show no greater hypertrophy effect.[12] The article also cites a twin study estimating that about 53 percent of variance in lean body mass is heritable, though it flags that source as weak.[12]

Grokipedia's summary of practice lists compound lifts as the core of training, 10 to 20 sets per muscle group per week, 7 to 9 hours of sleep, creatine monohydrate, weekly weigh-ins, and adjusting intake by a couple of hundred kcal when progress is too slow or too fast.[2] It describes the transition to a cut as beginning with a small deficit, aiming for roughly 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight loss per week with protein kept high.[2] Wikipedia notes that creatine is a popular bodybuilding supplement, and that studies show no metabolic advantage of eating 5 to 7 meals over 3.[1]

One summary says early scale increases partly reflect water stored with glycogen, and that an intermediate gaining 6 kg from 74 to 80 kg would need several months on a clean bulk, longer than on a dirty bulk, though its stated timelines conflict between sections.[2] The same source says that unlimited calories do not produce unlimited muscle, that returns diminish above a moderate surplus, and that intermediates can still gain meaningful muscle.[2]

Wikipedia says males gain muscle more easily than females on average, with about 60 percent more muscle mass.[12] Its hypertrophy article gives no rate of gain, so the per-week and per-year figures above come from the Grokipedia summary alone.[2][12]

The idea of a deliberate mass-building phase grew out of bodybuilding culture. Eugen Sandow, born in 1867 and called the father of modern bodybuilding, organised what is believed to be the first major bodybuilding competition at the Royal Albert Hall on 14 September 1901, with Sir Arthur Conan Doyle among the judges.[1][13] The International Federation of Bodybuilding was founded by Joe and Ben Weider in 1946, the Mr. Olympia contest began in 1965, and the 1977 film Pumping Iron brought the sport to wider audiences.[1] Grokipedia says off-season bulking became standard in the 1970s and 1980s.[2]

Terms such as clean and dirty bulking spread through bodybuilding and fitness forums, and later through looksmaxxing communities, where the emphasis is on appearance rather than competition: staying lean enough that the face and waist look defined while the shoulders, back and arms grow.[4][5]

A 2023 parallel-groups trial in Sports Medicine - Open by Helms and colleagues randomised 21 resistance-trained people, 17 of whom completed, to maintenance energy intake, a moderate surplus of about 5 percent, or a high surplus of about 15 percent, with resistance training three days per week for eight weeks.[3] There was no clear evidence of group differences in biceps, triceps or quadriceps thickness or in squat strength; the high-surplus group gained more bench-press strength than the others and increased skinfold thickness more than maintenance, while the moderate group showed weaker evidence of more skinfold gain than maintenance. Body mass change strongly predicted skinfold change and only weakly predicted biceps thickness change. The authors concluded that faster weight gain mainly raised fat gain rather than muscle thickness or strength, with possible slight biceps benefit, and noted limits in the sample and design, including losses of participants to COVID-19.[3]

A 2019 review by Slater, Dieter, Marsh, Helms, Shaw and Iraki in Frontiers in Nutrition examined whether an energy surplus is required to maximise skeletal muscle hypertrophy. The authors say the surplus needed for muscle gain is unknown, that textbook estimates counting only the energy stored in new tissue likely ignore other energy costs and metabolic responses, and that these estimates have not been validated in resistance-trained people; they discuss how much extra energy to eat, where it should come from and when, and identify gaps in the research.[8]
No trial was found that studies lean bulking as practised in looksmaxxing forums, including its effect on facial appearance.

Wikipedia says a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more fat.[1] Grokipedia lists poorly managed bulks as able to produce disproportionate fat gain, joint strain and overtraining, and says dirty bulking can raise cholesterol and triglycerides, while clean bulking reduces but does not eliminate these effects.[2] Progress is slower, and the 2023 trial suggests that body mass gain and fat gain are tightly linked.[3] Wikipedia also notes a long-standing diversity of views on protein and meal frequency, and that the line between natural and drug-assisted physiques is sometimes blurred by influencers who do not state which they are.[1]

A looksmax.org user at 155 lb asked whether a 500 kcal daily surplus would let him reach 165 lb without getting "chubby", saying he looks worse if he bloats; replies in the thread included suggestions of performance-enhancing drugs and peptides, which the poster declined.[4] A teenager who had cut from 165-170 lb to 140 lb asked whether to start a lean bulk or cut longer, worried about losing definition and regaining fat.[5] Another thread asked which supplements to use during a summer lean bulk, and others ask whether to lean bulk after a cut or to run a short lean bulk to regain lost muscle.[7][9]

A recurring theme is facial leanness: posters want muscle without the facial fat that any surplus can bring, and they discuss whether a natural lifter must choose between a thin build and a softer one.[5] On the T Nation forum, a contributor described a "300 calorie surplus of carbs" as a neutered approach that works for some natural lifters but is the exception.[10]

lore.intro: Forum discussion centres on how to gain muscle without losing facial definition, and whether a surplus will inevitably add facial fat.[4][5]

claims.claim: A small surplus (around 500 kcal) lets you add muscle without getting fat
claims.believers: Posters planning a lean bulk propose a modest daily surplus to gain a few pounds without bloating.[4]
claims.experts: In an 8-week trial, a 15 percent surplus added more skinfold thickness than maintenance without clear muscle thickness differences, while a 5 percent surplus showed only weak evidence of added skinfold.[3]

claims.claim: Natural lifters are stuck choosing between looking skinny and looking soft
claims.believers: One poster says a natural trainee in a permanent lean bulk will always carry some bloating and fat.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says bulks add fat in proportion to surplus size and duration and that competitors alternate bulks and cuts.[1]

claims.claim: A long cut damages metabolism and makes regaining fat likely
claims.believers: A teenager who cut for 2.5 months says he is scared of regaining fat because the cut may have affected his metabolism.[5]
claims.experts: No trial has tested this claim in forum-style lean bulkers.

claims.claim: A clean bulk is a better route to a good-looking physique than a dirty bulk
claims.believers: Lean-bulk advocates say a slow, controlled surplus avoids the long cut and the soft look that follow a dirty bulk.[2][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and Grokipedia describe dirty bulking as faster but fattier, and the 2023 trial links faster weight gain to more fat gain without clear muscle advantages.[1][2][3]

claims.claim: More calories always means more muscle
claims.believers: Dirty-bulk practitioners say a large surplus speeds up gains and is psychologically easier.[1]
claims.experts: Grokipedia says gains level off above a moderate surplus, and the Slater review says the surplus needed for muscle is unknown.[2][8]

claims.claim: Drugs are the only way to look lean while bulking
claims.believers: Replies in a looksmax.org lean-bulk thread respond to a 500 kcal plan by suggesting steroids or a growth-hormone-releasing peptide; the original poster declines.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes steroids are Schedule III in the U.S. since 1990 and that many natural federations test competitors; it describes widespread use among professionals.[1]

card.summary: A small calorie surplus aimed at adding muscle while limiting fat gain; slower than a dirty bulk.
card.note: Slower gains; forum users worry about gaining facial fat during any surplus.

quick.overview:
A lean bulk is a bulking phase using a modest calorie surplus, often described as 250 to 500 kcal per day above maintenance, with the goal of gaining muscle while adding as little fat as possible. It is the counterpart of the dirty bulk.

On looksmaxxing forums, users commonly ask whether a lean bulk will make them look fat or bloated, and how to balance muscle gain against facial leanness.
quick.mechanism: Calorie intake is set slightly above maintenance alongside progressive resistance training, with weekly weight tracking used to keep gains slow. A Grokipedia summary cites targets of about 0.25 to 0.5 kg per week and protein of 1.6 to 2.2 g/kg per day.
quick.risks: Slower progress and some unavoidable fat gain are the main caveats described. Early weight gain includes glycogen and water. No safety concerns specific to modest surpluses are noted in the sources.
